scenario: Today's embodied track asks which defaults in the data, the body, and the heat quietly get written into the policy. Bimanual demonstrations can be captured without occupying the target robot and then retargeted to a new body, and continual learning can use an evolving knowledge space without growing parameters. Pauses and detours in the collection interface are remembered by the policy, while parallelizing body-part control can shorten completion time substantially. The limit on sustained walking is often the hottest motor, not the battery; writing a body schema into the vision-action interface lets a smaller model emit action chunks faster. A tool-center-point representation unifies tracking and generation, and near-human-speed kinesthetic teaching pushes bimanual success above four fifths. Geometry supervision transfers unseen robot-skill combinations, a faster generalist begins to drive an arm directly, and the data factory can be handed to an agent started with two prompts.

papers.title: HandUMI: A Modular Hand-Worn Parallel-Jaw Interface for Robot-Free Bimanual Data Capture
papers.authors: Brik Meza, Leonardo Perez, Alvaro Mendoza-Li, Aniela Ubillus, Mitshell Ramos, Raul Bastidas, Mauricio Olivera, Bryan Bastidas
papers.abstract: HandUMI captures robot-free bimanual demonstrations with a hand-worn parallel-jaw interface. Swappable fingertips match the robot's installed gripper; Quest/PICO controllers track hands and encoders measure aperture. Robot-agnostic recordings are retargeted by inverse kinematics to seven simulated bimanual arms (median position error $\leq 1.2$ mm; $\leq 4.7$% of episodes rejected). On bimanual towel folding, 562 robot-free demonstrations train policies on real PiPER arms: ACT succeeds in 12/20 attempts and fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ in 7/20; ACT on the first 101 and base $\pi_{0.5}$ each succeed in 0/20. Hardware and software are open source (Apache-2.0), and a pair costs USD 557 with Quest 3S, excluding the optional ZED Mini and host computer. Project website: https://murobotics.ai/research/handumi.
papers.summary: Bimanual demonstrations usually occupy a robot during collection, and the motions are hard to move to a new body. A hand-worn parallel-jaw interface uses swappable fingertips to match the robot gripper, tracks the hands with headset controllers, and measures aperture with encoders. Bimanual demonstrations can therefore be captured without a robot and then retargeted by inverse kinematics to seven simulated bimanual arms, with median position error of at most 1.2 millimeters. On real PiPER arms folding a towel, an ACT policy trained on these robot-free demonstrations succeeds in 12 of 20 attempts, while the same policy trained on only an earlier slice of the data succeeds in none. The hardware and software are open source, and a pair with a Quest 3S stays inexpensive. For labs that need more bimanual data, ==demonstrations need not be bound to the target robot first.==

papers.title: Continually Evolving Skill Knowledge in Vision Language Action Model
papers.authors: Yuxuan Wu, Guangming Wang, Zhiheng Yang, Tianchen Deng, Maoqing Yao, Brian Sheil, Hesheng Wang
papers.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models show promising knowledge accumulation ability through pretraining, yet continual learning remains challenging. Existing continual imitation learning (CIL) methods often require additional parameters or modules, limiting scalability for large VLA models. We propose Stellar VLA, a knowledge-driven CIL framework without parameter growth, featuring two variants: T-Stellar for task-centric modeling and TS-Stellar for hierarchical modeling of reusable skills across tasks. Stellar VLA jointly optimizes task representations and a self-evolving knowledge space, with knowledge-posterior-guided expert routing using knowledge relations and Top-$K$ semantic embeddings for task specialization. Experiments on LIBERO demonstrate strong performance against VLA and CIL baselines with only 1\% replay. Dual-arm real-world experiments validate knowledge transfer across embodiments and scenes. TS-Stellar excels in hierarchical manipulation, while visualizations demonstrate knowledge retention and task discovery.
Project Page: https://stellarvla.github.io/.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action models can accumulate knowledge in pretraining, but continual learning remains hard. Existing continual imitation methods often add parameters or modules, which does not scale well for large models. A knowledge-driven framework with no parameter growth jointly optimizes task representations and a self-evolving knowledge space, and routes experts using a knowledge posterior over relations and semantic embeddings for task specialization. It has two forms: one that is task-centric, and one that models reusable skills across tasks in a hierarchy. On LIBERO, the method stays strong against vision-language-action and continual-imitation baselines with only 1% replay, and dual-arm real-world experiments validate knowledge transfer across embodiments and scenes. The hierarchical variant is stronger at hierarchical manipulation, and visualizations show knowledge retention and task discovery. For robot models that must keep adding skills, ==a knowledge space can evolve without growing parameters to remember old tasks.==

papers.title: Hidden Variables Behind Real-Robot Data Quality: Lessons from Hundreds of Thousands of Hours
papers.authors: Maniformer Real-World Manipulation Team, Che Tsang Calvin, Xingyu Chen, Bowen Jiang, Naixiang Gao, Xiongfeng Cai, Enlin Gu, Ruiying Li, Peize Li, Mianrui Zhu, Haomiao Zhang, Xin He, Minhui Yu, Jun Zhao, Zihao Zhu, Yang Chen, Jingmei Jin, Keru Zhou, Chen Wang, Chang Zhou, Zhiwen Hou, Di Yang, Wenjun Sun, Fan Yang, Liyan Zhang, Yi Lu, Haojun Ma, Jun Zhu, Pengxin Zha, Zhaosheng Wang, Xin Zhao, Xindong He, Chiming Liu, Jianheng Song, Jiayao Ma, Maoqing Yao, Guanghui Ren, Qian Wang, Wei Shan, Yang Yang, Li Liu, Wenhao Wang
papers.abstract: As real-robot data collection scales, collection-system design shapes both operator efficiency and the behaviors learned by robot policies. Workspace limitations, control-interface friction, and latency can introduce pauses, detours, and corrective motions into otherwise successful demonstrations. We investigate these effects across embodiment, teleoperation control, and data consistency, combining a kinematic study of 25 dual-arm robots, controlled teleoperation experiments, and real-robot evaluation of fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ policies. The embodiment study shows that positional reachability overstates orientation-aware task coverage and that modest shoulder motion can substantially expand the effective workspace. Teleoperation experiments show that parallelizing body-part control reduces task completion time by 43-53%, while compliant control improves success and reduces peak contact forces on constrained and contact-rich tasks. Policy-learning experiments show that demonstrations must capture the visual information underlying action choices: active-search demonstrations improve arm-selection accuracy from chance (50%) to 100%. Calibration experiments reveal that mixed-calibration training data remain usable in our tested configurations when an inference-aligned subset is retained, whereas inference-time miscalibration causes all 30 trials to fail. Policies also retain approximately 90% of the extra path length in detour-contaminated demonstrations, showing how inefficient operator motions persist in learned behavior. Together, these findings connect collection-system design to demonstration quality and downstream policy execution. They motivate evaluating effective workspace, control efficiency, observation completeness, calibration alignment, and motion quality before scaling collection, and addressing system-induced compensations at their source.
papers.summary: As real-robot data collection scales, workspace limits, control-interface friction, and latency can write pauses, detours, and corrections into demonstrations that still count as successful. One study looks at these hidden variables across embodiment, teleoperation control, and data consistency, combining a kinematic study of 25 dual-arm robots, controlled teleoperation experiments, and real-robot evaluation of fine-tuned policies. Parallelizing body-part control cuts task completion time by 43% to 53%, and compliant control improves success while reducing peak contact forces on contact-rich tasks. Policies also keep about nine tenths of the extra path length in detour-contaminated demonstrations, so inefficiencies in the collection system are remembered by the model. Task success alone does not reveal demonstration quality. Better real-robot data starts with seeing what the workspace and the interface actually write into the trajectory.

papers.title: From Temperature-Limited to Battery-Limited Legged Locomotion
papers.authors: Raphaël Ségas, Balázs Opra, Léo Ghafari, Thomas Stewart
papers.abstract: On legged robots, sustained locomotion often ends in thermal shutdown rather than battery depletion: the heat of walking concentrates in a few joint motors, which overheat long before the battery is empty. We train thermally aware locomotion policies by reinforcement learning without ever observing temperature, and demonstrate this on a Unitree Go2 quadruped. We first identify a coupled 13-node lumped RC thermal network, fitted on two runs of a single robot and calibrated against the measured electrical power, that predicts all twelve motor temperatures with a mean RMSE below 1 $^\circ$C across different robot instances, gaits, payloads, and speeds. Under a sustained gait, the temperatures the motors will settle at follow directly from the gait-averaged squared torques and joint speeds. Our core contribution is a reward that drives down the hottest predicted asymptotes: thermal time constants exceed the credit-assignment horizon of reinforcement learning by orders of magnitude, but predicted asymptotes respond to torque and joint speed within a single gait cycle, so the policy learns to lower and spread heat with no temperature input. On the robot, the policy turns sustained locomotion from temperature-limited to battery-limited: with a 5 kg payload at 1 m/s, a learned baseline reaches thermal shutdown after 19 minutes (1.1 km), whereas our policy runs the battery down after 174 minutes (10.0 km) with its hottest motor 14 $^\circ$C below the shutdown threshold in a 26 $^\circ$C room; on an unloaded factory circuit with stairs and ramps, the baseline overheats after 25 laps (6.2 km), while our policy completes 47 (11.2 km) on one battery with 22 $^\circ$C of margin.
papers.summary: Sustained walking on legged robots often ends in thermal shutdown of a few joint motors, long before the battery is empty. One method trains thermally aware locomotion policies with reinforcement learning without ever observing temperature, and demonstrates this on a Unitree Go2 quadruped. A lumped thermal network, fitted on runs of a single robot and calibrated to measured electrical power, predicts all twelve motor temperatures with a mean error below 1 degree Celsius across robots, gaits, payloads, and speeds. Under load, a policy trained without thermal awareness hits thermal shutdown in about 19 minutes, while the thermally aware policy drains the battery after 174 minutes, still with headroom at the hottest motor. Sustained walking should reward lower predicted asymptotes of the hottest joints, not only whether the current gait can move.

papers.title: Body Schema Policy: Body as the Vision-Action Interface for Efficient Robot Loco-Manipulation
papers.authors: Lechen Zhang, Chenyuan Chen, Muxin Zhou, Zewen He, Yoshihiko Nakamura
papers.abstract: Currently, robots can learn whole-body loco-manipulation through scale: the strongest policies have billions of parameters and still need task-specific fine-tuning. Humans have limited processing capacity, yet learn and act efficiently through a body schema that organizes what they see and how they move. We introduce Body Schema Policy (BSP), an imitation learning policy that builds such a schema into the vision-action interface. Its latent body schema places joint and link tokens on the robot's kinematic tree, where learned screw motions carry features between links. Through body-queried vision, each body part retrieves its own visual evidence, which conditions the denoising of its actions. With this inductive bias, BSP returns an action chunk faster than any policy we compare. Compact, body-specific visual readouts also emerge without spatial supervision: manipulation commands depend strongly on task objects, while locomotion commands respond more broadly to the scene. On nine simulated Unitree G1 whole-body tasks, BSP matches the $\Psi_0$ humanoid foundation model with $75\times$ fewer parameters and nearly doubles Diffusion Policy's success. The same holds on a real G1 and a Fetch mobile manipulator.
papers.summary: Whole-body loco-manipulation can be learned by scale: the strongest policies have billions of parameters and still need task-specific fine-tuning. Humans have limited processing capacity, yet organize what they see and how they move through a body schema. An imitation-learning policy writes such a schema into the vision-action interface. Its latent body schema places joint and link tokens on the kinematic tree, and learned screw motions carry features between links. Each body part then retrieves its own visual evidence to condition the denoising of its actions. With this inductive bias, the policy returns an action chunk faster than any policy compared in the study. A model of about 35 million parameters matches a much larger baseline's success rate with 75 times fewer parameters, and nearly doubles Diffusion Policy's success. On an RTX 6000 Ada, a 16-step chunk takes only 13.9 milliseconds.

papers.title: TCP4D: A Unified Tool-Center-Point Tracking and Generation Model for Robot Manipulation
papers.authors: Haosong Peng, Xiangyang Liu, Zhengshen Zhang, Yunfeng Fan, Tianyu Qi, Xin Xia, Yufeng Zhan, Wenchao Xu
papers.abstract: Robot manipulation videos provide a rich visual experience, yet recovering robot action and gripper-state annotations from RGB observations still remains challenging. Using the embodiment-agnostic tool-center-point (TCP) pose as the action space, we present TCP4D, a unified model in which a shared 4D scene representation both tracks observed TCP motion and generates future TCP trajectories. Given a monocular video and initial 2D TCP queries, the tracker directly recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3) and gripper states alongside scene geometry and camera parameters. The generator samples local features from the same 4D representation along the recovered TCP tracks, then combines them with robot observations and language instructions to predict future TCP states. Our new cross-embodiment augmentation pipeline converts existing RGB videos into demonstrations for alternative embodiments by retargeting the recovered motion and synthesizing the corresponding observations, without recorded source-robot states. Experiments show that the tracker achieves absolute trajectory errors of 7.60 and 16.07 mm on DROID and RoboLab and adapts to a new embodiment with only ten demonstrations. The generator achieves 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin and outperforms well-established policy models on two real-world tasks, while joint training on source and augmented demonstrations improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.
papers.summary: Recovering robot actions and gripper states from manipulation videos is still hard, especially after the embodiment changes. A unified model uses an embodiment-agnostic tool-center-point pose as the action space, and a shared four-dimensional scene representation both tracks observed tool-center-point motion and generates future trajectories. Given a monocular video and initial two-dimensional queries, the tracker recovers metric poses and gripper states, along with scene geometry and camera parameters. The generator samples local features from the same representation along the recovered tracks, then combines them with robot observations and language instructions to predict future states. Tracking absolute trajectory error is 7.60 millimeters on DROID and 16.07 millimeters on RoboLab; as a manipulation policy, mean success on RoboTwin is 69.19%. Cross-embodiment augmentation can also turn existing videos into demonstrations for other robots.

papers.title: ALOHA Lightning: Learning Fast and Precise Manipulation
papers.authors: John Hua Yao, Qi Wu, Yihuai Gao, Chelsea Finn, Zipeng Fu
papers.abstract: Learning from human demonstrations has enabled robots to acquire a wide range of manipulation skills, but learned policies typically execute far slower than ordinary humans. This speed gap is mainly due to lack of an interface for collecting demonstration data at high speed, and the difficulty in training policies that can robustly execute high-speed motions. In this paper, we present ALOHA Lightning (Flash ALOHA), a system for learning fast and precise robotic manipulation. Our system uses kinesthetic teaching to intuitively collect near-human-speed demonstrations on a backdrivable bimanual platform, yielding natural and fast trajectories. We also present a learning pipeline that enables smooth high-speed execution through test-time action smoothing and aligns the visual data distribution between data collection and deployment with masking. Given 50 demonstrations for each task, ALOHA Lightning autonomously completes bimanual tasks such as ball tossing and catching, folding shorts, battery insertion, and bussing tables for over 80% success rates while close to human speed. Project website: https://flash-aloha.github.io/
papers.summary: Learning from human demonstrations has given robots many manipulation skills, but the learned policies usually run far slower than ordinary people. The gap comes mainly from the lack of an interface for collecting demonstrations at high speed, and from the difficulty of training policies that can execute fast motions robustly. A system for fast, precise manipulation collects near-human-speed trajectories by kinesthetic teaching on a backdrivable bimanual platform, smooths actions at test time, and uses masking to align the visual distribution between collection and deployment. With 50 demonstrations per task, it autonomously completes bimanual tasks such as tossing and catching a ball, folding shorts, inserting a battery, and bussing a table, at over 80% success and at speeds close to a human. Execution time can also be cut by more than half compared with teleoperation. Fast manipulation needs a near-human-speed demonstration interface first, then alignment of actions and vision at deployment.

papers.title: Zero-Shot Compositional Generalization for Embodied Manipulation
papers.authors: Baicheng Li, Wenkang Qin, Youqi Pan, Dongxiao Mao, Yukun Zhou, Chuanfu Shen, Dong Wu, Shunkai Zhou, Zike Yan, Wei Sui, Hongbin Zha
papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations are collected on different embodiments, leaving many robot-skill combinations unobserved. Pooling these data shares visual knowledge, while joint labels remain tied to the demonstrating kinematic chain. We propose a geometry-supervised training framework for zero-shot composition of familiar robots and skills. The central insight is that a demonstrated command provides a tool-space target for every robot that can realize it. Calibrated forward kinematics supplies this supervision to foreign native action interfaces without their joint labels for that skill. Native reconstruction retains demonstrated configurations, and positive reachability checks select targets for cross-robot supervision. A visual policy learns to predict shared actions and executes through the target robot's native decoder. During policy learning, one prediction receives geometric supervision through both source and foreign native realizations. Matched supervision controls, repeated policy training and evaluations across three backbones and two simulators demonstrate improved transfer to missing robot-task combinations.
papers.summary: Robot demonstrations are collected on different embodiments, so many robot-skill combinations are never observed. Pooling the data shares visual knowledge, but joint labels stay tied to the kinematic chain that produced the demonstration. A geometry-supervised training framework treats a demonstrated command as a tool-space target for every robot that can realize it. Calibrated forward kinematics then supplies this supervision to another robot's native action interface, without joint labels for that skill on the foreign body. Native reconstruction keeps demonstrated configurations, and reachability checks select targets for cross-robot supervision. A visual policy learns to predict shared actions and executes them through the target robot's native decoder. Across three backbones and two simulators, cross-robot supervision raises success on held-out combinations by 9.5 and 8.6 percentage points over source-only supervision.

papers.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics
papers.abstract: On the Artificial Analysis Robotics 0.1 benchmark, Gemini 4 Hydrogen controls a real 6-axis arm through eight everyday tabletop tasks.
papers.summary: General-purpose robots need spatial and embodied reasoning, but they also need to be fast and inexpensive enough to keep adjusting on a real arm until the job is done. Gemini 4 Hydrogen folds specialized skills from stronger embodied-reasoning models into a faster generalist: given a goal in plain language and a camera view, it plans the task, writes and runs control code, and keeps adjusting until the work is finished. On the Artificial Analysis Robotics 0.1 benchmark, it controls a real six-axis arm through eight everyday tabletop tasks, from pouring a drink to packing blocks into a box, and scores 58, similar to the stronger Argon model at a lower cost per token. A robotics plugin also gathers hardware onboarding, simulation, and control into one workbench, so a developer can go from a robot in a box to a working application in an afternoon. For anyone deploying embodied agents, ==speed and reasoning no longer have to live in two separate models.==

papers.title: Build Training-Ready Physical AI Datasets with Two Prompts in NVIDIA Cosmos
papers.abstract: Curate, augment, generate, and label physical AI data, orchestrated by your coding agent.
papers.summary: Training physical AI often stalls on data: curation, augmentation, generation, and labeling live in different tools, the engineering pipeline is long, and a coding agent can rarely orchestrate the whole chain at once. A path on NVIDIA Cosmos folds these steps into a flow that a coding agent can orchestrate, and starts it with two prompts, with the aim of producing training-ready physical AI datasets. The point is not another isolated generative model, but to connect curation, augmentation, generation, and labeling inside one orchestration, shortening the path from raw observation to data a policy can train on. For teams training robots or physical AI, data preparation itself can be agent-driven, rather than beginning as a manual pipeline that only human operators can run. How far two prompts will go still depends on the task and the source data, but the direction is to hand the data factory to an orchestratable agent.
